function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m sorry—I don’t currently have the ability to reach out over SSH or HTTPS to pull down a live copy of your repository (`git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs‑welcome.git`). Because of that limitation I can’t inspect the exact source tree you’re referring to, so I can’t automatically tailor a Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, or a GitHub Actions workflow to match whatever’s inside it.

What **can** happen here is that I’ll give you ready‑to‑copy examples that would normally fit a standard “Hello World” Node.js application. If you paste those into the appropriate places in your own repo, then you can manually adjust paths, ports, versions, etc., to suit your particular setup.

---

### 1️⃣ Suggested Dockerfile  
```dockerfile
# Use an official lightweight Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & lock first – ensures cached layers stay intact
COPY package*.json ./

RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Build step (if applicable) – comment out if unnecessary
# RUN npm run build

#########################
# Production Stage
#########################
FROM node:18-alpine

ENV NODE_ENV production
EXPOSE 3000          # <-- change to whichever port your server uses

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install only prod dependencies again (or copy from builder)
COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy built artifacts + source
COPY --from=builder /app/. .
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist    # <--- optional, remove if no dist folder

CMD ["node","server.js"]                # <-- replace with entry script
```

> *If your repo already contains a Dockerfile, feel free to merge the relevant parts above.*

---

### 2️⃣ Sample Kubernetes Deployment & Service  

Create two separate YAML files under e.g. `.kube/deploy.yaml` and `.kube/service.yaml`. Adjust names, labels, image tags, and resource limits as needed.

#### deploy.yaml
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-app      # <- update if you prefer another name
spec:
  replicas: 2                   # ← tweak replica count
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: nodejs-welcome-app
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: nodejs-welcome-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-container
        image: ghcr.io/<your-org>/nodejs-welcome:<tag>
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: node-env-secrets     # <-- optional secrets reference
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000           # <-- same as EXPOSE in Dockerfile
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 15
        livenessProbe:
          tcpSocket:
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          timeoutSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 3
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 128Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 250m
            memory: 256Mi
---
```

#### service.yaml
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer         # Change to ClusterIP / NodePort if required
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: nodejs-welcome-app
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                 # External port exposed by the Service
    targetPort: 3000         # Matches containerPort defined earlier
```

> *Tip:* You may combine both objects into one single file if you’d rather keep things tidy—just separate each object with `---`.

---

### 3️⃣ Example GitHub Actions Workflow (`ci.yml`)  

Place this under `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. Replace `<org>` and `<repo>` placeholders with your actual values.

```yaml
name: CI Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]

jobs:
  lint-test-build-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      packages: write       # Needed for GHCR pushes
      id-token: write       # For OIDC authentication (optional)

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:14
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: test_user
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password123
          POSTGRES_DB: test_db
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5
        ports:
          - 5432/tcp

    steps:
      - name: Checkout Repo
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version-file: '.nvmrc'   # or specify directly: '20.x'
          cache: npm

      - name: Cache NPM Dependencies
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-npm-

      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Lint Code
        run: npx eslint src/**/*.ts

      - name: Run Tests
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgresql://test_user:password123@localhost/test_db
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Application
        run: npm run build

      #### Optional: Publish Docker Image to GHCR
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build Docker Image
        run: |
          IMAGE_NAME="ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY}"
          TAG="${GITHUB_SHA::7}"                     # Short SHA
          echo "${IMAGE_NAME}:${TAG}"
          docker buildx bake \
              --set *.platform=${DOCKER_PLATFORM:-linux/amd64} \
              --push \
              --output=image=${IMAGE_NAME}:${TAG}

      - name: Deploy to K8s (Optional)
        uses: azure/k8s-set-context@v2
        with:
          kubeconfig-value: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
          context-name: my-cluster
        continue-on-error: true
```

*Key points*

| Step | Purpose | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| `services.postgres` | Spin up Postgres locally for tests | Remove if you rely on other DBs |
| `cache.npm` | Reuse dependency layer across jobs | Improves speed |
| `buildx bake` | Multi‑arch builds & automatic push | Requires `Dockerfile.buildkit` style layout |

Feel free to delete or adapt any section that doesn’t apply to your stack.

---

### How to get everything onto GitHub

Once you’ve added the three new files (and possibly modified an existing Dockerfile), simply do:

```bash
git add Dockerfile .kube/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Docker/K8s/GitHub Action scaffolding"
git push origin main
```

That will trigger the newly configured pipeline immediately.
